pron_note: Also spelled exorcize; the noun is exorcism (EK-sor-siz-uhm).
means:
To **drive out an evil spirit** by ritual, prayer or command — and, far more often on the GRE, to **rid yourself of something that haunts you**: a memory, a guilt, a reputation, an old influence that still has a grip.

The figurative sense carries the ghost with it. You don't *exorcise* clutter or spare furniture; you exorcise what clings — something unwanted, faintly shameful, and hard to shake. It also implies effort and something like ceremony: writing the book, burning the letters, winning the rematch. Compare plain *remove* (mechanical) or *dispel* (an illusion simply evaporates) — exorcising is a **struggle against a thing that resists leaving**.
trap: ⚠️ **exorcise ≠ exercise.** One letter apart, opposite worlds: **exorcise** (with an **o**) casts out demons; **exercise** works the body or *uses* a right ("exercise caution", "exercise the option").
trick_line: Look inside: ex**ORC**ise — you're kicking the **orcs** out of the house.
trick_unpack: The hidden ORC is only in the demon-word, never in *exercise*, and it captures the sense of expelling something monstrous that won't leave on its own.
sentences: The memoir was less a confession than an attempt to **exorcise** a childhood she had never been able to speak of aloud.
Beating them in the final finally **exorcised** thirty years of losing to that lot.
in_the_wild: **The Exorcist** (1973) — the priest is there to *exorcise* the demon, which is exactly the job description.
etymology: Greek **ex-** ("out") + **horkos** ("oath") → *exorkizein*, literally "to bind by oath" — the exorcist expels the spirit by **swearing an oath at it** ("I command you, in the name of…"). That's why the word implies a formula, not just a shove.
one_line: Drive out an evil spirit — or a haunting memory.
